why_section.title: Why DevOps Consulting Matters for B2B
why_section.subtitle: Software delivery speed has become a board-level metric. The companies that ship daily — and recover from failure in minutes — outpace competitors running weekly release trains. DevOps consulting engagements translate that ambition into pipelines, platforms, and culture that compound.
why_section.paragraph_1: Most enterprise engineering organizations did not get here by accident — they grew through acquisitions, hiring waves, and product pivots that left the delivery toolchain heterogeneous. Jenkins running alongside GitHub Actions. Helm charts checked into the same repo as Terraform. Production access scattered across four ticketing systems. CI/CD modernization is the deliberate work of consolidating that estate into a single, opinionated delivery platform that every engineer can use without filing a ticket.
why_section.paragraph_2: The numbers justify the investment. Google's DORA research consistently shows that elite performers deploy 208 times more frequently than low performers, with 7x lower change failure rate and 2,604x faster recovery from incidents. Closing even a third of that gap typically requires two compounding moves: a fully automated CI/CD pipeline that takes a commit to production with no human gate, and a platform engineering layer that gives every developer a paved road for environment, secrets, and observability.
why_section.paragraph_3: Platform engineering changes the economics of delivery. When self-service provisioning replaces change boards for routine work, engineering velocity stops being a function of headcount. GitOps adoption turns cluster state into a versioned artifact that can be reviewed, rolled back, and audited the same way application code is. Infrastructure as code makes every environment reproducible, every drift detectable, and every change visible. These are not abstract benefits — they show up directly in MTTR, deployment frequency, and the change failure rate that boards now track.
why_section.paragraph_4: The wrong move is buying tools without an architecture. Stacking ArgoCD on top of a manual change process creates Git theatre, not GitOps. Adopting Kubernetes without a platform layer turns every team into an accidental cluster operator. Barbuk sequences the work: assess the delivery value stream, design the target pipeline, build the platform foundation, migrate workloads to it, and embed SRE practices that keep the system healthy under production load. The result is a delivery platform that scales with the engineering organization, not against it.

process.title: Our DevOps & CI/CD Modernization Approach
process.subtitle: A five-phase engagement refined across 50+ B2B modernization programs — designed to move delivery from manual to automated, from teams-of-heroes to platform-enabled product engineering.

steps.title: Delivery Value Stream Assessment
steps.text: We map every commit-to-production path, identify manual gates and bottlenecks, and benchmark your current state against DORA four-key metrics. The output is a prioritized target architecture with a sequenced modernization roadmap tied to measurable engineering outcomes.

steps.title: Target Pipeline & Platform Design
steps.text: We design the target CI/CD architecture, choose between GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or Jenkins, and define the platform engineering layer that will wrap every cluster. Decisions are documented, justified, and reviewed with your engineering leadership before any code is written.

steps.title: Platform Foundation Build
steps.text: We stand up the platform foundation: GitOps controllers, IaC modules, secret management, observability stack, and DevSecOps scanning. Foundations are built once and reused by every application team that joins the platform — the single biggest force-multiplier in the engagement.

steps.title: Pipeline Migration & Paved Roads
steps.text: We migrate one team at a time onto the new pipeline and platform. Each migration includes a paved-road template, hands-on enablement, and a hypercare window. We do not migrate all teams simultaneously — sequential migration lets us stabilize each cohort before the next onboarding.

steps.title: SRE Practices & Continuous Improvement
steps.text: We embed SRE practices: SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, blameless post-mortems, and a continuous improvement cadence for the platform itself. The engagement ends when your engineers run the platform without us, with documented runbooks and an SRE operating model.

case_study.title: Case Study: Manufacturing Company Modernizes CI/CD and Achieves DORA Elite
case_study.subtitle: How a European manufacturing company moved from weekly, manual deployments to 15-minute on-demand releases and cut change failures from 40 percent to 5 percent.
case_study.challenge: The engineering organization ran a single shared Jenkins instance inherited from a 2014 acquisition, with manual approval gates at every stage. Production deploys consumed an entire Friday every week, change failures averaged 40 percent, and rollback required a 6-hour war room. Product teams treated release days as code red, and quarterly roadmap commitments slipped by months because of deployment risk.
case_study.approach: We designed a trunk-based, GitOps-led delivery platform: GitHub Actions for CI, ArgoCD for cluster sync, Terraform for infrastructure, and a Backstage-based internal developer platform sitting on EKS. We migrated teams one cohort at a time, instrumented every stage with OpenTelemetry, and stood up an SLO-driven release process with progressive delivery through Argo Rollouts.
case_study.before: Weekly 3-hour production deploys, 40 percent change failure rate, 6-hour rollback, manual change advisory board approval for every release.
case_study.after: On-demand 15-minute deploys from main branch, 5 percent change failure rate, automated rollback under 90 seconds, fully self-served pipelines with policy gates only on regulated workloads.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Common questions B2B engineering leaders ask before starting a DevOps consulting engagement.

items.question: What is the DevOps consulting engagement model?
items.answer: We run a fixed-scope discovery and roadmap phase first — typically 3 to 4 weeks — followed by a multi-month delivery phase with a dedicated senior team. The discovery phase produces a measurable baseline, a target architecture, and a sequenced roadmap. Delivery proceeds in cohorts with explicit success criteria per cohort. Most engagements run 6 to 12 months end-to-end; some companies continue on a managed platform SRE basis afterwards.

items.question: How long does CI/CD modernization take?
items.answer: A focused CI/CD modernization for a single application team can be completed in 6 to 8 weeks. An enterprise-wide program covering 15 to 30 teams typically runs 9 to 14 months when sequenced cohort-by-cohort. Platform engineering layers take longer because they wrap every other team — plan for 6 to 9 months before measurable DORA metric movement appears across the engineering organization.

items.question: Do you work with our existing Jenkins or GitHub Actions?
items.answer: Yes — we rarely recommend ripping out working tooling. Our default is to keep your existing CI engine (Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or Buildkite) and modernize the surrounding pipeline: shared libraries, environment promotion, secrets integration, security gates, and progressive delivery. We migrate tools only when the existing engine cannot meet a specific architectural requirement, and we handle the migration when that case arises.

items.question: What is the ROI of platform engineering?
items.answer: Most B2B platform engineering engagements reach payback within 12 to 18 months. The largest return drivers are: engineering hours saved per sprint on environment provisioning and CI maintenance (typically 15 to 25 percent of senior engineer time); reduction in incident MTTR through better observability; faster onboarding of new engineers onto the paved road; and reduced cost of compliance through policy-as-code and shift-left scanning. We build a business case during the discovery phase with conservative, your-numbers modeling.

items.question: How do you handle legacy monolith deployments?
items.answer: Legacy monoliths stay on their existing deployment process — we wrap, do not replace. Typical pattern: keep the monolith on its current release cadence, surround it with a platform layer for new microservices, and progressively extract well-bounded capabilities into containerized services that consume the monolith through stable APIs. Argo Rollouts and feature flags let us canary individual extracted services without touching the monolith deployment cadence. We have shipped this pattern at multiple manufacturing and financial services clients.
